title: Record It When It Happens, Capitalise Only What Builds
summary: Accrual accounting records costs when work is done, not when cash moves. Capitalised costs go on the balance sheet as work in progress until the asset is finished, and only costs that build the asset belong there. The owner's monthly cost report shows budget, committed, incurred, paid and forecast final cost.
body:
An owner's books record what happened when it happened, not when the money moved, and they put the cost of building an asset on the balance sheet rather than through profit. Get those two habits right and your monthly report tells the truth; get them wrong and it tells a story.

Recall

Q. Last week Vera named three levels of assurance. Which one adds no checking at all?

A. A compilation. An audit gives reasonable assurance, a review gives limited assurance, and a compilation simply assembles management's numbers.

Q. In Week 10, Sage defined net operating income. What is left out of it?

A. Debt service, depreciation and income tax. NOI describes the building's operations, not its financing, accounting or tax.

Q. In Week 4 you learned the two forces that set your alertness. What are they?

A. Sleep pressure, which builds the longer you are awake, and the body clock, which swings through the day. Shift work puts them out of step.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia here. Last week was about reading statements. This week is about producing them as an owner. Every month on a project you will report to a lender, to investors and to yourself. That report must answer three questions: what has the project cost so far, what will it cost at the end, and has anything changed? The two ideas in this lesson, accrual and capitalisation, decide whether those answers are right. A third idea, work in progress, is where the answers live on your balance sheet.

Accrual: record it when it happens

In plain English, accrual accounting records an expense when you incur it and revenue when you earn it, regardless of when cash moves. Cash accounting records only when money changes hands. Most frameworks require accrual for any company of size, and lenders almost always expect it.

The professional framing: at the end of each month you ask, "What work was done for us this month that we have not yet been billed for, or have been billed for but not yet paid?" Work done and not yet billed is recorded as an accrued liability. Work billed and not yet paid sits in accounts payable. Both are costs of the month, even though no cash has left.

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. In March your architect completes $50,000 of design work. The invoice arrives in April and you pay it in May. On a cash basis, March shows nothing and May shows $50,000. On an accrual basis, March shows the $50,000 cost and a $50,000 liability; April moves it from accrued to payable; May pays it and clears the liability. Only the accrual version tells you, at the end of March, what the project really cost to date.

On a construction site this matters every month. Your contractor's pay application usually covers work done up to a cut-off date and arrives some days later. If you wait for the invoice, your cost report always runs weeks behind the site. The discipline is to estimate the work done but not yet billed, from the site's own progress records, and to accrue it.

Capitalised costs: building an asset is not an expense

To capitalise a cost is to record it as part of an asset on the balance sheet instead of as an expense in the income statement. When you build a rental building, the land, the construction, the design fees, the permits and, under many frameworks, part of the interest on the construction loan become the cost of the building. That cost is then depreciated, an expense spread over the building's useful life, once it is in use.

The professional framing: a cost may be capitalised only if it is directly attributable to bringing the asset to the condition and location needed for its intended use. Marketing a rental building, general office overhead, and costs after the building is ready for use are usually expensed, not capitalised. The precise test, and especially the treatment of borrowing costs, differs by framework; verify it against the framework your statements use and with your accountant.

Say that out loud now. Accrue the work when it is done. Capitalise only what builds the asset.

Why it matters: capitalising moves cost out of this year's profit and into an asset. Capitalise too much and profit looks better than it is, and the asset is carried at more than it cost to build. Day 2 shows a company that did exactly that, at scale.

Work in progress: where it all sits

For an owner, work in progress, often called construction in progress, is the balance sheet account that accumulates every capitalised cost of a project until it is finished. It is not yet depreciated, because the asset is not yet in use. When the building is ready, the balance moves to buildings or investment property, and depreciation or the chosen measurement model begins.

Contractors use the phrase differently: for them it usually means the gap between revenue recognised and amounts billed on their contracts. Know which meaning someone intends.

Second worked example, hypothetical. Eighteen months into a project, your work in progress account holds land of $2,000,000, hard costs of $3,000,000, soft costs of $800,000 and capitalised interest of $200,000: a total of $6,000,000. Your income statement for the same period shows only $150,000 of expense, for marketing and company overhead. A reader who looks only at profit sees a company that spent $150,000. The balance sheet shows the $6,000,000 asset and, on the other side, the loan and equity that paid for it.

Reporting: the five columns

The owner's monthly cost report turns all of this into one page. Each cost line carries five figures. Budget: the approved figure. Committed: what you have signed contracts or orders for. Incurred: work actually done to date, including accruals. Paid: cash that has left. Forecast final cost: incurred plus what remains to be committed and spent, including contingency. The variance between forecast final cost and budget is the number your lender and investors care about most. The paid column is the one beginners stare at, and it is the least informative of the five.

A quick illustration on one line, hypothetical. Mechanical works: budget $1,200,000; committed $1,150,000 under a signed subcontract; incurred $600,000 to date including $80,000 accrued for this month; paid $480,000. The subcontract is half complete and the site team expects $90,000 of known changes still to be priced. Forecast final cost is $1,150,000 plus $90,000, which is $1,240,000, a $40,000 overrun on budget, visible today even though less than half the money has been paid. A report showing only the paid column would show this line comfortably under budget for months.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cost report that reports cash paid as if it were cost incurred. It runs weeks behind the site, hides overruns until the invoices arrive, and makes the forecast final cost a guess. The control: accrue monthly from site progress records, reconcile the incurred column to the contractor's latest pay application, and reforecast the final cost every month, line by line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner capitalises everything spent on the project, including marketing, overhead and costs after completion, because it makes the yield on cost and the profit look better. The professional writes a capitalisation policy before the first invoice, has the accountant approve it, and follows it even when it hurts.

Callback

In Week 10, yield on cost was stabilised NOI divided by total project cost. Total project cost is, in practice, your work in progress balance at completion plus any costs still to come. If that balance includes costs that should have been expensed, the yield looks fine while the real cost of the project is higher than you think. Your yield on cost is only as honest as your capitalisation policy.

Recap

Accrual records costs when work is done, not when cash moves. Capitalisation puts the cost of creating an asset on the balance sheet, and only costs that build the asset belong there. Work in progress holds those costs until completion. The monthly cost report shows budget, committed, incurred, paid and forecast final cost, and the forecast is what matters.

Next: Ford, with Cole assisting, on WorldCom and the ordinary costs it recorded as assets.
checklist: Accrue work done but not yet billed at every month end, from site progress records.
Write a capitalisation policy, approved by your accountant, before the first invoice.
Expense marketing, general overhead and costs after the asset is ready for use, unless your framework says otherwise.
Confirm how your framework treats construction loan interest.
Report budget, committed, incurred, paid and forecast final cost on every cost line.
Reconcile the incurred column to the contractor's latest pay application.
Reforecast final cost line by line every month.
head: Field checklist
speak: As an owner, my books record costs when the work happens, not when I pay. That is accrual accounting. If my architect does 50,000 dollars of work in March and I pay in May, the cost belongs in March. Each month end I estimate work done but not yet billed and accrue it. Second, capitalisation: the costs of creating a building, land, construction, design and, under many frameworks, some construction interest, go on the balance sheet as work in progress, not through profit. Only costs that build the asset belong there. Marketing and overhead are usually expensed. Third, reporting: every cost line shows budget, committed, incurred, paid and forecast final cost. The forecast final cost against budget is what my lender and investors care about. I write a capitalisation policy before the first invoice, because my yield on cost is only as honest as that policy.
terms: Accrual accounting — recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves.
Capitalised cost — a cost recorded as part of an asset on the balance sheet rather than as an expense in the income statement.
Work in progress — for an owner, the balance sheet account that accumulates the capitalised costs of a project until it is ready for use; also called construction in progress.

hostile.q: Your cost report shows you have spent 4 million dollars. Your contractor says the work in place is worth 5 million. Which is it?
hostile.a: Probably both, measured differently. Four million is what we have paid. The contractor's figure is work done, including its latest unbilled month and the retainage we hold. My report carries an incurred column that accrues work done from the site records and reconciles to the latest pay application, so I would expect incurred to be close to five million. If it is not, the gap is a question I will resolve this week, with the pay application and the site progress records side by side.

title: WorldCom: When Operating Costs Became Assets
summary: WorldCom recorded billions of dollars of ordinary operating costs as capital assets, turning losses into reported profit, until its internal auditors traced the entries in 2002 and the company filed for bankruptcy that July. The root cause was a capitalisation policy management could override, and incentives that rewarded overriding it.
body:
In 2002 WorldCom admitted it had recorded billions of dollars of ordinary operating costs as if they were capital assets, turning losses into reported profit. It is the clearest case on record of what happens when capitalisation becomes a lever for hitting a target.

Recall

Q. On Day 5 last week, what was the NPV of a $5,000,000 sale in year 2, at 12 percent, on $1,000,000 of land and $3,000,000 of construction?

A. About $307,000. Delaying the same sale to year 3 turned it to about minus $120,000.

Q. In Week 10, Stuyvesant Town was bought on the strength of what kind of income?

A. Future income from moving rent-regulated apartments to market rents, which credit conditions and a court ruling prevented.

Q. Week 4's failure case was the Exxon Valdez. What did the safety board name among the probable causes?

A. Fatigue and excessive workload among the crew, alongside other factors.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Cole assisting on audit and integrity. You will soon have a capitalisation policy of your own, and every month you will decide whether a cost builds an asset or is simply a cost. WorldCom shows that this small, technical decision can be the whole difference between a company that reports profit and one that reports losses. The facts below come from public reporting, the company's own disclosures and the later investigations. I give no figure I cannot stand behind; where the amounts were large, I say so without precision.

Step 1: Timeline

WorldCom was an American telecommunications company that grew rapidly in the 1990s through acquisitions, including the much larger long-distance carrier MCI in 1998. When the telecommunications boom turned to bust around 2000 and 2001, revenue growth slowed and costs did not. In 2002 the company's internal audit team, working largely on its own initiative, found entries that had moved ordinary operating costs into capital accounts. In June 2002 the company announced it would restate its results. In July 2002 it filed for bankruptcy protection, at the time the largest such filing in American history. Its chief executive and chief financial officer were later convicted or pleaded guilty to criminal charges.

Step 2: Key decisions

The central decision was to reclassify what the industry called line costs, fees paid to other carriers for access to their networks, from operating expense to capital expenditure. Those costs bought nothing lasting; they were the ordinary cost of carrying traffic each month. Capitalising them took them out of the income statement and spread them over many years as depreciation. Profit rose immediately and the balance sheet swelled with an asset that did not exist.

Step 3: Assumptions

The working assumption appears to have been that the downturn was temporary, that revenue would recover, and that the entries could be absorbed or reversed later without anyone noticing. Underneath sat a second assumption: that a large company's capital spending is too big and too technical for anyone to question individual entries. Both were wrong.

Step 4: Incentives

The company was valued by the market on its earnings and its growth. Executive wealth was tied to the share price, and senior management had borrowed heavily against their shares, by public accounts. Analysts watched one ratio closely, line costs as a share of revenue. Every incentive pointed toward reporting a lower cost ratio and a higher profit, and the capital account was the place where cost could be made to disappear.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The signs were visible to anyone who looked for them in the right place. The company's margins held up while its competitors' fell. Capital spending was large and rising in a market where telecom companies were cutting it. Entries were made at the top of the organisation, in round amounts, without the supporting invoices and approvals that capital spending normally carries. Some staff raised concerns. The external auditor did not detect it; the internal auditors did, by tracing entries back to their source.

Say that out loud now. If margins hold when everyone else's fall, find out which costs moved to the balance sheet.

Step 6: Point of no return

The first reclassification was the point of no return. Once a quarter's reported profit depended on cost moved to the balance sheet, the next quarter needed the same entry, plus more, simply to keep the numbers from falling. Each entry made the eventual correction bigger and the decision to stop harder. That is the same ratchet you saw at Carillion, with a deliberate act at its start instead of an optimistic estimate.

Step 7: Root cause

Cole's reading: the root cause was a capitalisation policy that could be overridden by the people it was meant to constrain, combined with incentives that rewarded doing so. A rule that management can change quietly to hit a number is not a rule.

The developer's version

Composite example, hypothetical round numbers. A small developer owns a newly finished rental building with NOI of $900,000. Lease-up has been slow, so for twelve months after completion the building's leasing costs, its marketing and $150,000 of loan interest are all quietly added to the project's cost instead of being expensed. The yield on cost falls only slightly on paper, from 7.5 percent to about 7.4 percent, because the cost base looks larger and nobody objects. But the income statement shows the building breaking even when it is in fact losing money every month, and the investor report says the same. When the investors' accountant reviews the file a year later, the restatement erases what looked like a year of profit and the developer's credibility with it.

The control is the same at any size. A written capitalisation policy, approved by your accountant, that states when capitalisation stops: usually when the asset is ready for its intended use. Supporting documents for every capitalised entry. And a second person, even a part-time bookkeeper, who must approve any entry that moves a cost from expense to capital.

How the internal auditors found it

The method that uncovered WorldCom is one you can run yourself, every month, in under an hour. Pick a handful of capitalised entries at random, and a handful of the largest. For each one, trace it back to its source: the invoice, the contract it was charged under, the approval, and the asset it created. An entry that cannot be traced to a document and a physical asset is not capital spending, whatever account it sits in. Second applied example, hypothetical: your project's work in progress rises by $300,000 in a month when the site report shows little progress. Tracing finds $180,000 of company overhead allocated to the project by a spreadsheet formula nobody reviewed. It comes out, the month's expense rises, and the cost report is honest again before anyone outside the company has relied on it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a capitalisation decision made by the same person whose results it flatters. The control is separation: one person proposes, another approves, against a written policy, with documents.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks capitalisation is a technical detail for the accountant. It is a judgement about whether money spent created something lasting, and the owner is responsible for it.

Callback

In Week 3 you learned that people respond to how they are paid. WorldCom is that principle at its most destructive: the people who controlled the entries were the people rewarded by the result. When you design your own reporting, ask who benefits from each judgement call, and make sure that person is not the only one making it.

Recap

WorldCom moved ordinary operating costs into capital accounts, inflating profit and assets, until its own internal auditors traced the entries in 2002. The root cause was a policy that management could override and incentives that rewarded overriding it. Rule 12: a cost goes on the balance sheet only if it creates or improves an asset under a written policy my accountant has approved; I never change the policy to hit a number, and no capitalisation entry is approved by the person it flatters.

Next: Priya on capitalised interest, the cost report and what your lender reads in it.
checklist: Write a capitalisation policy that states when capitalisation starts and stops.
Have your accountant approve the policy before the first invoice.
Require supporting documents for every capitalised entry.
Separate the person who proposes a capitalisation from the person who approves it.
Stop capitalising when the asset is ready for its intended use.
Ask why margins hold when competitors' margins fall.
Watch for capital spending rising when the market is cutting it.
head: Field checklist
speak: WorldCom was a large American telecom company. When growth slowed around 2000, it began recording ordinary operating costs, fees paid to other carriers for network access, as capital assets. That took them out of the income statement and spread them over years, so losses appeared as profits and the balance sheet carried assets that did not exist. Its own internal auditors traced the entries in 2002. It restated in June and filed for bankruptcy in July, and its senior executives were later convicted or pleaded guilty. The root cause was a capitalisation policy that the people it constrained could override, and incentives that rewarded them for doing it. On my projects, a written policy approved by my accountant decides what is capitalised, capitalisation stops when the asset is ready for use, and no entry is approved by the person it flatters.
terms: Capital expenditure — spending that creates or improves a lasting asset and is recorded on the balance sheet.
Operating expense — the ordinary cost of running a business in the period, recorded in the income statement.
Restatement — the correction of previously issued financial statements found to be materially wrong.

hostile.q: Your building has been open a year. Why is its interest still in the project cost?
hostile.a: It should not be, and I would expect your question. Our policy, approved by our accountant, stops capitalisation when the building is ready for its intended use. If you have found interest capitalised after that date, it is an error and I will have it expensed and the reports restated. I will send you the policy, the completion date and the entries since then so you can check every one.

rule: Rule 12: A cost goes on the balance sheet only if it creates or improves an asset under a written policy my accountant has approved; I never change the policy to hit a number, and no capitalisation entry is approved by the person it flatters.

title: Cost to Complete and the Loan in Balance
summary: Capitalised interest belongs in total project cost, and leaving it out overstates yield on cost and the spread. Forecast final cost is incurred to date plus a bottom-up cost to complete, and the in-balance test asks whether undrawn loan plus remaining equity covers that cost. The Wealth Ledger treats an overrun guarantee as a personal liability waiting to arrive.
body:
The costs you capitalise and the costs still to come decide two numbers your lender watches every month: your true yield on cost and whether the loan is still in balance. A cost report that understates either one is borrowing against money you do not have.

Recall

Q. Last week, in the credit review, what did Roman hand the lender to explain profit up and cash down?

A. A one-page reconciliation from net income to the change in cash, tying to the dollar, built from three items.

Q. In Week 10, Roman showed that a cap rate move hits equity first. Why?

A. Because the loan stays the same size while value changes, so the whole change in value lands on the smaller equity slice, magnified by leverage.

Q. In Week 4 you priced a tired mistake. What two ways did the lesson use?

A. As expected cost, probability times impact, and as carrying cost, the extra time and interest an error adds.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. Nadia gave you accrual, capitalisation and the five-column cost report. My job is to show you what those columns do to the money. A construction lender will read your cost report before every draw, and it reads two things: the forecast final cost, and whether the money left to spend still covers the work left to do. Investors read the same report to see whether their return is holding. If your report is wrong by the time they read it, you have a financing problem, not just an accounting one.

Capitalised interest belongs in the cost

Interest on the construction loan is a real cost of creating the building, and under many frameworks part of it is capitalised. Whatever the accounting treatment, it belongs in your total project cost when you measure yield on cost, because you had to pay it to get the building.

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Stabilised NOI is $600,000. Land, hard and soft costs total $8,000,000. Interest during construction is $400,000. Measured on $8,000,000, yield on cost is 7.5 percent. Measured honestly on $8,400,000, it is about 7.14 percent. Against a market cap rate of 6 percent, the development spread falls from 150 basis points to about 114. A third of the margin you thought you had was interest you left out of the denominator. Week 13 called finance costs the line that grows while you wait; here is where it shows up in the return.

Forecast final cost and cost to complete

Cost to complete is everything still to be spent to finish the project. The professional framing builds it from the cost report, line by line: committed costs not yet incurred, plus uncommitted costs still to be bought, plus the contingency you expect to use. Forecast final cost is incurred to date plus cost to complete.

Second worked example, hypothetical. Budget $10,000,000. Incurred to date, including accruals, $4,000,000. Committed but not yet incurred, $3,500,000. Uncommitted work still to buy, estimated at $2,200,000. Contingency you expect to need, $500,000. Cost to complete is $3,500,000 plus $2,200,000 plus $500,000, which is $6,200,000. Forecast final cost is $4,000,000 plus $6,200,000, which is $10,200,000. You are forecasting a $200,000 overrun with 60 percent of the cost still to come.

Notice which number would have hidden it. Paid to date might be $3,600,000, comfortably under the budget to date. Only the forecast column shows the overrun, and it shows it now, when there is still time to cut scope, rebid a package or raise equity calmly.

What the lender checks: is the loan in balance?

Most construction loan agreements contain an in-balance requirement: the loan money not yet drawn, plus the equity you have yet to contribute, must at all times be enough to pay the cost to complete. If it is not, you must put in the difference, usually before the next draw is released. This is commercial practice written into loan agreements, not a standard, and Week 40 covers it in depth.

Continue the example. Undrawn loan, $5,500,000. Equity still to be contributed under the plan, $400,000. Together, $5,900,000. Cost to complete, $6,200,000. The loan is out of balance by $300,000. Until you cover that gap, the lender may refuse to fund the next draw, and your contractor's next pay application goes unpaid.

Say that out loud now. Undrawn loan plus remaining equity must cover cost to complete. If not, the gap is mine to fund before the next draw.

This is why an honest forecast is in your own interest. A forecast that hides the $200,000 overrun keeps the loan in balance on paper for a month or two, and then the gap appears all at once, larger, with less time to fix it and a lender who no longer trusts your reports.

Where the cost report meets the draw

Each month your draw request asks the lender for money against the same numbers. The lender's monitor will compare the draw to the cost report and to the contractor's pay application, and expect them to agree: work incurred this month, less the retainage you are holding back, less anything already funded. Hypothetical: the pay application shows $600,000 of work this month, you hold back 10 percent as retainage, which is commercial practice and varies by contract and jurisdiction, so the contractor is due $540,000, and that is the hard-cost figure in your draw. If your cost report says $650,000 incurred because you accrued an extra $50,000 the contractor has not yet claimed, say so in a note. Three documents that disagree without an explanation are how a draw gets delayed by a month.

How the best do it

Experienced owners and their cost consultants share a practice a small developer can copy: a monthly cost-to-complete review, line by line, signed by the cost consultant and the project manager, with every change to forecast final cost explained in one sentence. Movements between contingency and cost lines are logged, never netted silently. The lender's monitor sees the same file the owner does. Nothing about it is expensive; it is a habit and a signature.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. If you have guaranteed completion or cost overruns, the $300,000 in-balance gap above is not the project's problem; it is yours, and it can arrive with a few weeks' notice. Carry your project interests on your personal balance sheet at cost or at a conservative value, never at the pro forma value, and list beside each one the largest call it could make on you. Then test it against your liquidity floor. A guarantee is a liability that does not appear on your balance sheet until the day it does. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting cost to complete be a plug, the figure that makes the report balance, rather than a bottom-up estimate. The control: build it from committed, uncommitted and contingency every month, reconcile incurred to the contractor's pay application, and run the in-balance test yourself before the lender does.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reports paid against budget and calls the project on track. The second mistake is to measure yield on cost without interest, because interest feels like financing rather than building.

Callback

In Week 13 you learned that every estimate must carry its class, its date and its contingency. Cost to complete is an estimate too. Each month, say how much of it is committed and therefore firm, and how much is still an estimate. A $6,200,000 cost to complete that is 56 percent committed is a very different risk from one that is 10 percent committed.

Recap

Interest is a real cost of creating the building, and leaving it out of total cost overstates yield on cost and the spread. Forecast final cost is incurred plus a bottom-up cost to complete. The in-balance test asks whether undrawn loan plus remaining equity covers cost to complete, and any gap is yours to fund before the next draw.

Next: Elias on why your tax ledger and your book ledger treat the same costs differently.
checklist: Include interest during construction in total cost when measuring yield on cost.
Build cost to complete from committed, uncommitted and expected contingency.
Calculate forecast final cost as incurred plus cost to complete.
Run the in-balance test yourself before every draw.
State how much of cost to complete is committed.
Log every movement between contingency and cost lines.
List the largest personal call each guaranteed project could make on you.
head: Field checklist
speak: What I capitalise and what is still to come decide two numbers my lender watches. First, yield on cost. Interest during construction is a real cost of creating the building. Six hundred thousand dollars of NOI on 8 million is 7.5 percent, but on 8.4 million, with interest, it is about 7.1, and a third of my spread disappears. Second, the loan balance. Cost to complete is committed plus uncommitted plus expected contingency. With 4 million incurred and 6.2 million to come, my forecast final cost is 10.2 million against a 10 million budget. The in-balance test asks whether undrawn loan plus remaining equity covers cost to complete. If 5.9 million is available against 6.2 million needed, I must fund 300,000 before the next draw. So I build cost to complete from the bottom every month, and I run the in-balance test before my lender does.
terms: Cost to complete — the estimated amount still to be spent to finish a project: committed but not incurred, plus uncommitted, plus expected contingency.
Forecast final cost — incurred cost to date plus cost to complete; the owner's best estimate of what the project will finally cost.
In-balance requirement — a loan condition that undrawn loan funds plus remaining equity must always cover the cost to complete.

hostile.q: Why does your forecast final cost go up this month when you paid less than budget to date?
hostile.a: Because paid to date measures cash, not cost. The forecast is built from committed contracts, uncommitted work still to buy and the contingency we expect to need, and this month two packages priced above their budget lines. That moved forecast final cost up by 200,000 dollars. The loan is now out of balance by 300,000, and I will contribute that equity before the next draw. The schedule of each movement is in the report.

title: Book and Tax Are Two Different Ledgers
summary: Accounting rules and tax rules treat the same project costs differently, especially during construction. Capital spending is generally recovered over time, timing differences create deferred tax, and whether a building is inventory or a capital asset changes the character of the profit. Every specific rule must be verified against the primary source.
body:
Your accountant keeps two sets of rules for the same project: the accounting rules that produce your financial statements and the tax rules that produce your tax return. The same cost can be treated differently in each, and the difference changes when you pay tax, sometimes how much.

Recall

Q. At the end of last week, Kema's Red Pen found a summary that counted condo deposits as cash available for the next project. Why was that wrong?

A. Deposits are commonly held in trust for buyers and are not the developer's money to spend; counting them as available is wrong and may breach trust and deposit rules.

Q. In Week 10, Vera taught you to read four facts before an appraisal's number. What are they?

A. The client, the intended use, the effective date and the assumptions.

Q. In Week 4, what did the lesson say the law asks instead of how tired you were?

A. What you owed, what you knew and what you signed. Fatigue is rarely a defence; the duty and the signature remain.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Elias here. Developers often assume their accounts and their tax return say the same thing. They usually do not. The book profit in your statements and the taxable income on your return can differ for years at a time on the same project, and the difference determines when tax falls due. Get it wrong and you either pay tax earlier than you needed to or, worse, claim a deduction the law does not allow. I teach concepts and how to think. I do not state any rate, threshold or section here, and every specific rule must be verified against the primary source and with a qualified tax adviser before you rely on it.

Two ledgers, two purposes

In plain English, accounting rules try to show economic reality to investors and lenders. Tax rules decide what the government taxes and when, and they serve policy goals as well as measurement. So the two will often disagree about timing, and sometimes about whether a cost counts at all.

The professional framing uses one distinction that both systems share in some form: capital versus current spending. Current spending, sometimes called a revenue expense, is the ordinary cost of earning income in the year, and is generally deductible against that year's income. Capital spending creates or improves a lasting asset, and is generally not deducted at once. Instead it becomes part of the asset's tax cost and is recovered over time, through tax depreciation, or at the end, when the asset is sold. Tax systems often have their own name and their own schedules for tax depreciation; Canada's is called capital cost allowance, for example, and its classes and rates are set by regulation. Verify the current rules against the primary source before you rely on them.

Costs during construction

The period of construction is where the two ledgers diverge most. Many tax systems require certain costs incurred while a building is being built, which might otherwise look like ordinary expenses, such as interest on money borrowed to build or property taxes on the land during construction, to be added to the cost of the building rather than deducted as incurred [unverified — confirm independently]. Some allow particular soft costs to be deducted. The accounting framework may treat the same item differently again. The practical question to ask your adviser is not "is it deductible?" but "when, in which ledger, and added to what?"

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers and a hypothetical tax rate of 25 percent chosen only to make the arithmetic visible; it is not the rate in any real jurisdiction. In year one you spend $100,000 on a cost that your tax adviser confirms you may deduct immediately for tax, while your accounting framework requires it to be capitalised into the building. Your book profit is unaffected this year. Your taxable income is $100,000 lower, so tax this year is $25,000 lower. That is a timing difference: later, as the building is depreciated in your books but the cost has already been deducted for tax, the position reverses. The total tax over the life of the asset may be the same; the timing is not, and timing is money, as Nadia showed you on last week's Day 5.

Say that out loud now. Book and tax can disagree about when a cost counts. Ask when, in which ledger, and added to what.

Deferred tax: the bridge between the ledgers

Because the two ledgers disagree about timing, financial statements under many frameworks carry a deferred tax balance: the tax that will become payable, or recoverable, later, when today's timing differences reverse. You do not need to calculate it. You need to recognise it, so that a large deferred tax liability on a balance sheet is read as a real future cost, not an accounting oddity. When you value a company or a building held in a company, ask what deferred tax sits inside it.

Inventory or capital: the question of character

The second big divergence is character. The same building can be held as inventory, something you build in order to sell, or as a capital asset, something you hold to earn rent. A condo project built for sale is typically treated as inventory, and the profit on sale as business income. A rental building held for the long term may be treated as capital property, and the gain on an eventual sale may be taxed differently, with earlier tax depreciation potentially recaptured. Which one applies is decided on facts and intention, and those can be tested by a tax authority years later. This is a concept, not a conclusion for any jurisdiction; Week 23 maps the real estate taxes and Week 24 covers how authorities look at substance over form.

Second worked example, hypothetical. You build 20 units planning to rent them, and record the project as a capital asset. Two years later, values have risen, and you sell all 20 units individually within months. A tax authority may ask whether you were really a builder-seller all along, which could change the character of the profit and the tax treatment of the deductions you claimed. The defence is evidence: board minutes, financing terms, leasing records and correspondence, made at the time, that show the intention you claimed. Vera's lesson last week applies; a record made later is weaker than one made at the time.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser, licensed accountant or tax lawyer, in each jurisdiction where the project or its owners are taxed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is claiming a tax deduction for a cost because your books expensed it, or capitalising for tax because your books capitalised it, without checking that the tax rules agree. The control: before the first invoice, ask your tax adviser for a written note on how each major cost category is treated for tax during construction, and keep it with your capitalisation policy.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the tax return is the accounts with a few adjustments. The professional keeps a reconciliation of book profit to taxable income every year and knows which differences are timing and which are permanent.

Callback

On this week's Day 1, Nadia asked you to write a capitalisation policy before the first invoice. Write its tax twin at the same time. The two policies answer the same question, does this cost build the asset, under two different rulebooks, and the reconciliation between them is where most construction-period tax errors are found.

Recap

Book and tax ledgers serve different purposes and often disagree about timing. Capital spending is generally recovered over time, and many systems require certain construction-period costs to be added to cost. Timing differences create deferred tax. Whether a building is inventory or capital changes the character of the profit. Verify every rule against the primary source.

Next: Nadia working backward from a finished building's cost to the monthly entries that built it.
checklist: Ask your tax adviser for a written note on each major cost category's tax treatment during construction.
Keep the tax note beside your capitalisation policy.
Reconcile book profit to taxable income every year.
Label each difference as timing or permanent.
Read any deferred tax balance as a real future cost.
Record your intention for each project, inventory or capital, in documents made at the time.
Verify every rate, threshold and rule against the primary source before relying on it.
head: Field checklist
speak: My accounts and my tax return follow different rulebooks. Accounting tries to show economic reality; tax decides what is taxed and when. Both distinguish current spending, generally deducted in the year, from capital spending, generally recovered over time through tax depreciation or on sale. During construction they diverge most, and many tax systems require certain costs, such as some interest and property tax during construction, to be added to the building's cost. So I ask my adviser when a cost counts, in which ledger, and added to what. Timing differences create deferred tax, which is a real future cost. And character matters: a building built to sell is usually inventory, and one held for rent may be a capital asset, with different tax on the profit. That is decided on facts and intention, so I record my intention at the time. Every rule I verify against the primary source.
terms: Capital versus current spending — the distinction between spending that creates a lasting asset, recovered over time, and ordinary spending deductible in the year.
Timing difference — a difference between book and tax income that reverses over time, so it changes when tax is paid rather than how much.
Deferred tax — the tax that will become payable or recoverable in future when today's timing differences reverse.

hostile.q: Your accounts capitalise construction interest. Why does your tax return deduct some of it?
hostile.a: Because the two ledgers follow different rules, and I would not assume they match. My tax adviser's written note sets out how each cost category is treated for tax during construction, and our annual reconciliation of book profit to taxable income shows every difference and whether it is timing or permanent. I will give you both documents, and if any deduction is not supported by the note, we will correct it.

title: Working Backward From a Finished Building's Cost
summary: A reverse-engineered calculation: start from a completed building's 12,000,000 dollar capitalised cost and trace it to land, hard, soft and interest components, outside documents, cash paid, retainage and accruals. The same backward walk locates a forecast overrun in the packages still to be bought.
body:
Start from the finished number, the cost of the completed building on the balance sheet, and work backward until every dollar is traced to cash paid, cash still owed or a cost that should never have been there. If it does not trace, the number is wrong.

Recall

Q. On Day 1, what are the five columns of the owner's cost report?

A. Budget, committed, incurred, paid and forecast final cost.

Q. In Week 10, Sage worked backward to the residual land value. What is subtracted from the finished value to reach it?

A. Every cost except land, and the developer's required profit.

Q. In Week 4 you planned a sharp two o'clock meeting backward from the meeting time. What was the principle?

A. Plan the body like a schedule: start from the moment that matters and work back through sleep, caffeine and food so you arrive at your best, not by accident.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia here. This is an even-numbered week, so we reverse engineer. When a project finishes, someone will look at the cost of the building on your balance sheet: an investor, a lender refinancing it, a buyer's accountant, or a tax authority. The question will always be the same: what is in that number, and can you prove it? The fastest way to answer is to take the finished figure apart, in a fixed order, until it reconciles to cash. Do it yourself before anyone else does.

The outcome we start from

Hypothetical round numbers. A rental building has just been completed. Your balance sheet now shows it at a capitalised cost of $12,000,000. The building's stabilised NOI is $900,000, so your reported yield on cost is 7.5 percent. You have the general ledger, the bank statements, the loan statements and the contractor's final pay application.

Step 1: Break the total into its components

From the work in progress ledger, the $12,000,000 is made up of land $2,500,000, hard costs $7,500,000, soft costs $1,400,000 and capitalised interest $600,000. Add them: 2.5 plus 7.5 plus 1.4 plus 0.6 is 12.0 million dollars. If the components do not add to the total, stop; something was posted to the asset without being coded to a cost line.

Step 2: Test each component against an outside document

Land: match $2,500,000 to the purchase agreement, the closing statement and the transfer costs your capitalisation policy allows. Hard costs: match $7,500,000 to the contractor's final pay application, including approved change orders, plus any direct owner purchases. Soft costs: match $1,400,000 to the consultant contracts and permit receipts.

Interest needs arithmetic. The loan statements show drawn balances that averaged about $6,000,000 over the two years of construction, at a hypothetical interest rate of 5 percent a year. Average balance times rate times years: $6,000,000 times 0.05 times 2 is $600,000. The capitalised interest is consistent with the loan. If it had been $750,000, you would look for interest charged after the building was ready for use, which your policy says should be expensed, or fees posted to the wrong line.

Say that out loud now. Every component of a finished cost must match a document outside my own ledger.

Step 3: Reconcile cost to cash

The bank statements show $11,250,000 paid out against the project. That is $750,000 less than the $12,000,000 cost. The difference must be cost incurred but not yet paid, and it must be identified line by line. Here: retainage, or holdback, of $500,000 still held back from the contractor under the contract, plus $250,000 of final invoices received and accrued but not yet paid. $11,250,000 plus $500,000 plus $250,000 is $12,000,000. Cost reconciles to cash.

Both items are liabilities on your balance sheet. Retainage will be released when the contract's conditions for release are met; the rules for when, and the lien or holdback regime behind it, depend on the jurisdiction and the contract, and Week 117 covers them. The point here is that they are owed, and your cash forecast must show them.

Step 4: Find what was spent and correctly kept out

The bank statements also show $150,000 that went out on the project but is not in the $12,000,000: $100,000 of leasing and marketing, and $50,000 of interest for the first month after completion. Your policy expenses both. Check that they really are in the income statement. A cost that left the bank and appears in neither the asset nor the income statement is the most dangerous kind; it means the ledger is missing something.

One more check sits in this step. Leasing commissions paid to brokers for signing tenants are treated differently across frameworks and policies; some carry them as a separate asset spread over the lease term, others expense them. Whichever your policy says, the question is the same: did the cost leave the bank, and does it appear exactly once, in the place the policy names? Ask your accountant which treatment your framework requires and write it into the policy.

Step 5: Reverse engineer the yield

Now see what a weaker policy would have done. If the $150,000 had been capitalised, the building would show a cost of $12,150,000, and yield on cost would be $900,000 divided by $12,150,000, about 7.41 percent, a small drop that looks harmless. But the income statement would have looked $150,000 better, and the asset would be carried above what it cost to build. In the other direction, if the $600,000 of interest had been left out entirely, the reported cost would be $11,400,000 and the yield would appear to be about 7.89 percent, overstating the margin by about 39 basis points. Both errors are found in exactly the same way: tracing the components.

Step 6: Work back to one month's entries

Finally, take one month and rebuild its entries, because that is where errors are made. In the final month the contractor's work was $250,000, invoiced but unpaid at month end. The entry: work in progress up by $250,000, with an accrued liability of $250,000 on the other side. When paid, the liability goes down and cash goes down by the same amount; the asset is untouched. If you find a month where work in progress rose but neither cash nor a liability moved, the entry was wrong.

Second worked example: working back from a forecast overrun

Hypothetical. Halfway through another project, your forecast final cost is $10,200,000 against a $10,000,000 budget. Work backward. Incurred is $4,000,000, so cost to complete is $6,200,000. Of that, $3,500,000 is committed, $500,000 is expected contingency, and $2,200,000 is uncommitted work. The uncommitted line was budgeted at $2,000,000. So the whole $200,000 overrun sits in packages not yet bought. That tells you where to act: re-scope or rebid those packages before you commit them, rather than chasing committed contracts that cannot change.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a finished cost that cannot be traced, because invoices were posted to the asset in bulk without coding, or because company costs were allocated to the project by formula. The control: code every invoice to a cost line when it is entered, and run this six-step trace at completion and at least once during construction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reconciles the total and stops. The professional reconciles the components, because errors in opposite directions can cancel in a total and survive inside it.

Callback

Last week, Vera taught that the statements are only as strong as the evidence behind each number. This is that lesson applied to the largest number on your balance sheet. A $12,000,000 building that reconciles to contracts, pay applications, loan statements and bank statements is a fact. One that reconciles only to your ledger is an assertion.

Recap

Start from the finished cost. Break it into components, test each against outside documents, reconcile cost to cash through retainage and accruals, confirm that expensed costs were kept out, recalculate the yield, and rebuild one month's entries. The same backward walk locates a forecast overrun in the packages you can still change.

Next: JAX, in the room presenting the monthly report to your investors.
checklist: Break the finished cost into components and check they add to the total.
Match each component to a document outside your own ledger.
Recalculate capitalised interest from average drawn balance, rate and time.
Reconcile cost to cash through retainage and accrued invoices.
Confirm expensed costs are in the income statement, not missing.
Rebuild at least one month's entries from source documents.
Code every invoice to a cost line when it is entered.
head: Field checklist
speak: I start from the finished number: a building on my balance sheet at 12 million dollars, with 900,000 of NOI, a 7.5 percent yield on cost. I break it into land, hard costs, soft costs and capitalised interest, and check they add to 12 million. I match each to an outside document: the purchase agreement, the final pay application, the consultant contracts. I test interest with arithmetic: a 6 million dollar average balance at 5 percent for two years is 600,000. Then I reconcile cost to cash: 11.25 million paid, plus 500,000 of retainage held and 250,000 of accrued invoices, is 12 million. I confirm that leasing costs and post-completion interest were expensed, not lost. And I rebuild one month's entries. A building that reconciles to outside documents is a fact; one that reconciles only to my ledger is an assertion.
terms: Retainage — a portion of each contractor payment held back until stated conditions are met; also called holdback.
Accrued liability — an amount owed for work or goods received but not yet invoiced or paid at the reporting date.
Reconciliation to cash — proving that a recorded cost equals cash paid plus identified amounts still owed.

hostile.q: Prove to me the 12 million dollar cost on your balance sheet is real.
hostile.a: Here is the trace. Twelve million is land, hard costs, soft costs and capitalised interest, each matched to the purchase agreement, the contractor's final pay application, the consultant contracts and the loan statements. The interest recalculates from the average drawn balance. Bank statements show 11.25 million paid; the remaining 750,000 is retainage and accrued invoices, both listed as liabilities. Leasing costs and post-completion interest were expensed under our written policy. You can pick any entry and I will show you its source document.

title: Telling Investors the Forecast Moved
summary: A scene on the monthly investor call: costs are ahead of the budget curve and the forecast final cost has risen. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state, plus this month's thread on reporting around a rotating shift schedule.
body:
Investors read a monthly report for one thing: whether their return is still on track. Show them the forecast final cost and the change since last month first, explain every movement in one sentence, and never make them discover an overrun you already knew about.

Recall

Q. On Day 2, what was the root cause at WorldCom?

A. A capitalisation policy that the people it constrained could override, combined with incentives that rewarded them for overriding it.

Q. In Week 10, JAX defended an exit cap rate to a sceptical partner. What did he refuse to do?

A. Defend a single number as a promise. He offered a range and showed the deal survived the downside.

Q. In Week 4 you learned to hold your state in a two o'clock meeting after night shifts. Name one technique.

A. Slow breathing with a longer out-breath, done while seated before the meeting; a practitioner habit, not medical advice.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, JAX here, on investors. Your investors gave you money on the strength of a pro forma. Every month after that, your report is the only window they have into whether you are managing it well. A good report builds the trust that gets you their next cheque. A report that hides a problem until it is too large to hide ends the relationship, even if the project eventually succeeds.

The scene

Hypothetical. You are eight months into a $10,000,000 rental project with three equity investors. The monthly call is with their representative, an experienced finance professional. Your report shows paid to date of $3,600,000, incurred of $4,000,000 and a forecast final cost of $10,200,000, up $200,000 from last month. The loan is out of balance by $300,000, and you have already told the lender you will fund it.

She opens: "Your incurred is four million against a budget-to-date of three and a half. Are we over?"

The question behind the question

She is asking three things. Is the overrun real or a timing difference? Is it going to grow? And will it come out of the investors' pocket, through a capital call or a reduced return? She is also testing whether you will tell her the truth when it is uncomfortable.

The lines to say

Bottom line first: "Two things. The incurred figure is ahead of the budget curve because steel arrived early; that is timing, not overrun. Separately, the forecast final cost rose $200,000 this month, because two packages still to be bought priced above budget. That is real, and I want to walk you through it."

Then the movement: "Contingency remaining covers $200,000 of it in the base case. The loan is out of balance by $300,000 until I contribute equity, and I will fund that from the developer's share, as the agreement provides, before the next draw. On today's forecast, the projected return moves down slightly but stays above the investors' preferred return. Here is the schedule."

Say that out loud now. Timing first, then the real movement, then who pays, then the return.

The lines never to say

  • "We're on budget." Not if the forecast final cost has moved. Say what moved.
  • "It's within contingency, so it doesn't matter." Contingency is the investors' money too; using it is a decision they deserve to see.
  • "We'll make it back on the next package." A hope is not a forecast.
  • Any explanation that changes from last month without saying it changed.

When to stay silent

After you say the forecast moved $200,000, stop. Let her absorb it and ask her own question. The urge to soften bad news with immediate reassurance makes it sound worse. Silence after a clear statement sounds like control.

Worked example: what the movement does to her return

Hypothetical. The project's stabilised value is $11,500,000. On the original $10,000,000 cost, created value was $1,500,000, 15 percent on cost. At $10,200,000, created value is $1,300,000, about 12.7 percent on cost. Say it in one sentence: "The overrun takes about $200,000 off created value; profit on cost goes from 15 percent to about 13, and the investors' return stays above their preferred return." If she asks what happens if the remaining uncommitted packages also come in 10 percent high, have the number ready: 10 percent of $2,200,000 is $220,000 more, created value falls to about $1,080,000, and you can say whether the preferred return still holds.

A second exchange

A second investor joins the call. "Your soft costs went up $40,000 this month. Are you charging your own company's overhead to the project?" This is Day 2's question in a friendly voice, and the right answer is a document. "No. Our capitalisation policy, approved by our accountant, capitalises only costs directly attributable to the building. The $40,000 is the structural engineer's change for the revised transfer beam, here is the invoice and the change order. Company overhead is expensed in the development company's own accounts. I'll send you the policy." Then offer more than she asked: "If it helps, you can pick any three entries each quarter and I will show you the source documents." An investor who has been invited to check rarely needs to.

After the call

Send a short written summary the same day: the forecast final cost, the movement and its reason, who funds the gap and when, the effect on the return, and anything you promised to send, with a date. Investors talk to each other. Make sure the version they repeat is the one you wrote, in your numbers, not the one each remembers.

Holding your state

Bad-news calls are where people speed up and over-explain. Write your first two sentences on a card and read them. Speak slower than feels natural. If you are challenged, acknowledge, bridge to the fact, answer: "That's a fair concern. What the numbers show is this." Practitioner habits, not rules.

Monthly thread: time and energy on a rotating shift schedule

Kema's thread for this month. Month-end reporting does not wait for your shift pattern. If the cost report is due on the third working day and you are coming off nights, the report will be written by a tired person unless you plan otherwise. Treat it like any other critical task from Week 4: schedule the accruals, the reconciliation and the forecast for your best alert window, not the end of a night block, and build the report from a checklist so fatigue cannot skip a step.

Two practical habits. Do the mechanical work, coding invoices and gathering pay applications, during low-alert hours, and save the judgement work, the forecast and the investor narrative, for high-alert hours. And never send an investor report in your red window. Draft it, sleep, read it once more, then send. If fatigue or sleep affects your health, check that with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the slow reveal: a $50,000 movement each month for four months, each explained away, until investors realise the project is $200,000 over and you knew in month one. The control is to report the forecast final cost and the cumulative change since the original budget on the first line of every report.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads with progress photos and finishes with costs. Investors want the reverse: cost and return first, progress as the evidence.

Callback

In Week 6 you learned the one-page memo, bottom line first. Your monthly investor report is that memo, repeated twelve times a year. The first line should be forecast final cost against budget, and the second line the change since last month.

Recap

Separate timing from real movement, say the real movement plainly, say who pays and what it does to the return, then stop. Put forecast final cost and cumulative change on the first line of every report. Plan reporting around your alert windows.

Next: Kema's week 12 review, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: Put forecast final cost and cumulative change since budget on the first line of every report.
Separate timing differences from real cost movements.
Say who pays for any movement and what it does to the return.
Prepare the downside number for the remaining uncommitted packages.
Stay silent after stating bad news clearly.
Never call a cost on budget when the forecast has moved.
Schedule judgement work on the report for your best alert window.
head: Field checklist
speak: On the investor call I lead with what they care about: is their return on track. I separate timing from real movement. Incurred cost ahead of the budget curve because steel arrived early is timing. A 200,000 dollar rise in forecast final cost because two packages priced high is real, and I say so plainly. Then I say who pays: contingency covers part, I fund the loan balance gap from the developer's share, and the investors' return stays above their preferred return. Then I stop and let them ask. I never say we're on budget when the forecast moved, and I never say we'll make it back later. I have the downside ready: if the remaining packages come in 10 percent high, here is the return. And I put forecast final cost and cumulative change on the first line of every report, written in my best alert window, not after a night shift.
terms: Budget curve — the planned pattern of spending over time, against which incurred cost is compared to separate timing from overrun.
Capital call — a demand that investors contribute additional equity under the terms of their agreement.
Cumulative change — the total movement in forecast final cost since the original approved budget.

hostile.q: Why should we believe this is the last overrun?
hostile.a: You shouldn't take it on faith. Here is what is still exposed: 2.2 million dollars of uncommitted packages, which is where this month's movement came from. If those come in 10 percent high, forecast final cost rises another 220,000 and the return is shown on page two. Everything else is committed under signed contracts. I'll report the forecast and the cumulative change on the first line every month, so you will see any movement the month it happens.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 12 Review: Owner Accounting and the Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions on accrual, capitalisation, Rule 12, forecast final cost, the in-balance test and book versus tax; a recap of the week; Cole's Auditor's Chair on a flawed monthly cost report; and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week was about producing honest numbers as an owner: accrue the work when it is done, capitalise only what builds the asset, and forecast the final cost from the bottom up. Today Cole reads a monthly report the way a hostile auditor would.

Recall

Q. On Day 3, what does the in-balance test compare?

A. Undrawn loan plus remaining equity, against the cost to complete. Any shortfall must be funded by the owner, usually before the next draw.

Q. In Week 10's review, what is the formula for profit on cost from yield on cost and the cap rate?

A. Yield on cost divided by the cap rate, minus one. A 7.5 percent yield against a 6 percent cap rate gives 25 percent.

Q. Week 4 closed with Rule 4. What does it say?

A. Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Why this matters

Kema here. Mr Shabazz, every report you send as an owner will one day be read by someone looking for what is wrong with it: a lender's monitor, an investor's accountant, an auditor or a tax authority. Week numbers divisible by four put Cole in the Auditor's Chair, so today you practise reading your own kind of document with their eyes, before they do.

The six questions

Question 1. Your architect finishes $50,000 of work in March, invoices in April and is paid in May. Under accrual accounting, which month carries the cost? Answer: March, the month the work was done. April moves it from accrued to payable; May pays it.

Question 2. What test decides whether a cost may be capitalised into a building? Answer: Whether it is directly attributable to bringing the asset to the condition needed for its intended use, under the framework you use. Marketing, general overhead and costs after the asset is ready for use are usually expensed.

Question 3. What does Rule 12 say? Answer: A cost goes on the balance sheet only if it creates or improves an asset under a written policy my accountant has approved; I never change the policy to hit a number, and no capitalisation entry is approved by the person it flatters.

Question 4. Budget $10,000,000, incurred $4,000,000, committed not incurred $3,500,000, uncommitted $2,200,000, expected contingency $500,000. What is the forecast final cost? Answer: $10,200,000, a $200,000 overrun, with cost to complete of $6,200,000.

Question 5. Undrawn loan is $5,500,000 and remaining equity is $400,000. Is the loan in balance? Answer: No. $5,900,000 against $6,200,000 leaves a $300,000 gap the owner must fund.

Question 6. Why can book profit and taxable income differ on the same project? Answer: Because accounting and tax follow different rules, especially on capital versus current spending and costs during construction. The differences are often timing, which creates deferred tax, and every rule must be verified against the primary source.

Say that out loud now. Accrue when it happens. Capitalise only what builds. Forecast from the bottom up.

Recap of the week

Nadia taught accrual, capitalisation, work in progress and the five-column cost report. Ford and Cole took apart WorldCom, where ordinary operating costs were recorded as assets. Priya showed that interest belongs in total cost and that the in-balance test makes an overrun yours to fund. Elias explained why book and tax disagree, and why character, inventory or capital, matters. Nadia traced a finished building's cost back to cash. JAX put you on an investor call where the forecast had moved.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Cole here. Read this hypothetical owner's monthly report as I would, assuming nothing and asking what each line hides. There are seven problems. Find them before reading on.

Month 14 cost report. Building completed in month 12. Paid to date $9,600,000 against budget $10,000,000: under budget. Cost to complete $400,000, being budget less paid. Capitalised this month: interest $45,000; leasing and marketing $30,000; development company office rent allocated $20,000. Contingency used: none, after transferring $250,000 from contingency into the hard cost line in month 9. No accruals this month as the contractor's final invoice has not arrived. Capitalisation entries prepared and approved by the development manager.

My reading. One: "paid against budget" is the wrong measure; it says nothing about cost incurred or forecast final cost. Two: cost to complete is a plug, budget minus paid, not a bottom-up estimate of what is still to be spent. Three: interest is still being capitalised two months after completion; under a typical policy capitalisation stops when the building is ready for use, so it should be expensed. Four: leasing and marketing are capitalised; under most policies they are expensed, or treated under a separate rule for leasing costs, but they are not building cost. Five: company office rent is allocated to the project, which is overhead, the WorldCom pattern in miniature. Six: "contingency used: none" is false in substance; $250,000 was moved into a cost line in month 9, so contingency was used and the report hides it. Seven: there are no accruals because an invoice has not arrived, so work done is missing from cost, and the same person prepares and approves the capitalisation entries, which defeats the control.

A bonus point for the careful reader: the report gives no forecast final cost at all. An auditor who sees no forecast will build one, and it will be less generous than yours.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week in two minutes to a board that understands business but not development accounting. Then compare with this model answer.

"Our project accounts follow three rules. First, we record costs when work is done, not when we pay, so our cost report keeps pace with the site rather than with the invoices. Second, we put on the balance sheet only the costs that build the building: land, construction, design and the construction interest our framework allows. Marketing and our own overhead are expensed. A written policy, approved by our accountant, decides, and the person whose results it affects does not approve the entries. Third, we forecast the final cost from the bottom up every month: what is committed, what is still to buy, and the contingency we expect to use. If the loan money left plus our equity does not cover the cost to complete, we fund the gap before the next draw. We report the forecast and its change on the first line of every report, so you hear about a movement the month it happens."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is knowing the rules and letting convenience bend them: capitalising one more month of interest, skipping an accrual because the invoice is late, netting a contingency transfer. Each is small; together they make a report that cannot survive an auditor. The control is the policy, the checklist and a second signature.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a cost report for whether it is under budget. The professional reads it for what it would take to prove each line, and whether the forecast is built or plugged.

Callback

Last week's Rule 11 said a reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing. This week's Rule 12 is its partner on the cost side: a reported asset that is not built from documented, attributable costs is a question too. Read together, they cover both halves of the statements: what you claim to have earned, and what you claim to own.

Recap

Accrue monthly from site records. Capitalise only what builds the asset, under a written, approved policy with separated approval. Forecast final cost from committed, uncommitted and contingency, and run the in-balance test yourself. Keep book and tax as two reconciled ledgers. Trace finished costs to outside documents. Tell investors the moment the forecast moves.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned to produce honest numbers as an owner. I record costs when work is done, not when I pay, so my cost report keeps pace with the site. I capitalise only what builds the asset, land, construction, design and the interest my framework allows, under a written policy my accountant approved, and the person it flatters never approves the entry. WorldCom showed what happens when ordinary costs are recorded as assets. I forecast final cost from the bottom up: committed, uncommitted and expected contingency. If undrawn loan plus remaining equity does not cover cost to complete, I fund the gap before the next draw. My tax ledger follows different rules, so I reconcile the two every year. At completion I trace the building's cost to outside documents and cash. And I tell investors the month the forecast moves.
terms: Plug — a figure forced to make a report balance rather than estimated on its own; a cost to complete calculated as budget minus paid is a plug.
Contingency transfer — moving budget from contingency into a cost line; it is contingency used, and must be reported as such.
Auditor's Chair — Cole's drill of reading a document as a hostile auditor would, assuming nothing and asking what each line hides.

hostile.q: Your report says no contingency used. Your month 9 report shows a 250,000 dollar transfer out of contingency. Which is true?
hostile.a: The transfer is the truth, and the wording in this month's report is wrong. Moving budget from contingency into a cost line is contingency used, and I will restate the contingency schedule to show the original amount, every transfer with its date and reason, and what remains. Going forward the report will show contingency drawn cumulatively, not just this month.
